items.definition: Implied volatility is the volatility input that, when plugged into an option pricing model like Black-Scholes, reproduces the option's observed market price.
items.core_idea: Because volatility can't be directly observed (unlike rates, prices, strikes, and expirations), it's backed out by iteratively guessing a volatility value, computing the model price, and comparing to the actual traded price until the two match.
key_points: All other Black-Scholes inputs are observable or easily estimated from the market or contract terms.
Volatility is the one input that must be inferred rather than observed.
The standard method is numerical: guess sigma, solve Black-Scholes, compare to market price, and refine the guess iteratively.
trading_implications: Traders quote and trade options in terms of implied volatility rather than dollar premium in many markets.

items.definition: An Asian option settles against the average price of the underlying over a defined period, rather than a single price observed at expiration.
items.core_idea: Averaging prices over time dampens the impact of any single day's price manipulation or abnormal move, making the option's settlement more resistant to gaming near expiration.
key_points: Also called average price options.
Commonly used in markets like crude oil where reducing sensitivity to expiration-day manipulation or noise is valuable.
trading_implications: Chosen specifically to reduce settlement risk from price manipulation or one-off spikes on the expiration date.

items.topic: Why Asian options have lower implied volatility
items.definition: Averaging a series of random prices produces a result with less dispersion (lower volatility) than any single price drawn from that same series.
items.core_idea: Because the settlement is an average rather than a single spot observation, the effective volatility priced into an Asian option is lower than that of an equivalent European option, making it cheaper for buyers and safer for sellers.
key_points: The statistical reduction in dispersion from averaging is the mechanical reason Asian options price with lower implied volatility.
Lower volatility pricing translates to lower premiums than a comparable European option.
This also makes the position less risky from the seller's perspective.
relationships: Follows from Asian option payoff definition
Affects premium relative to European options
trading_implications: Buyers pay less for Asian options than for comparable standard options because of the reduced effective volatility.
Sellers of Asian options take on less risk than sellers of comparable European options.
common_misunderstandings: One might assume an average-price option should price the same as a European option with the same underlying and strike; the averaging mechanically lowers effective volatility, so it does not.

items.definition: Asian options are approximated using a modified Black 76 formula with an adjusted volatility input, since the true distribution of an averaged price series is not exactly lognormal.
items.core_idea: The average of several lognormal price distributions is not itself lognormal, so exact closed-form pricing isn't possible, but a modified Black 76 approach with adjusted volatility gives a reasonably good approximation outside the delivery/averaging period.
key_points: Outside the delivery month, an adjusted-volatility version of Black 76 is used as an approximation.
Within the delivery month, part of the averaging period's prices are already known/observed, so the model must calculate the expected dispersion of the remaining unobserved prices.
As more of the averaging period's prices become known during the delivery month, expected volatility declines rapidly.
trading_implications: Risk on an Asian option should be expected to fall quickly as the delivery/averaging month progresses and more of the settlement prices are locked in.
common_misunderstandings: The author notes the average of lognormal distributions is not itself lognormal — an exact analytic solution isn't available, only an approximation.

items.definition: The volatility smile is the pattern seen when implied volatility is plotted against strike price: out-of-the-money and in-the-money options tend to show higher implied volatility than at-the-money options.
items.core_idea: Because the assumption that prices are lognormally distributed breaks down most for options with extreme strikes or long maturities, the market prices these options with higher volatility than at-the-money options to compensate for that extra model risk, producing the smile shape when graphed.
key_points: All corrections for imperfections in the option model (e.g., inaccuracy of the lognormal assumption) show up as adjustments to the volatility input, since every other input is directly observable.
Options with high or low strikes, or very long maturities, are most affected by the lognormal assumption being inaccurate.
These options are priced with different (typically higher) volatility than at-the-money options to account for that risk.
Implied volatility is observed in the market by backing out volatility from the Black Scholes equation using actual traded option prices and known inputs.
relationships: Related to lognormal price distribution assumption
trading_implications: Traders should expect deep out-of-the-money or long-dated options to trade at higher implied volatility than at-the-money options, not the same flat volatility.
common_misunderstandings: Assuming a single flat volatility should apply across all strikes; the smile reflects that the lognormal assumption is worse at extreme strikes/maturities.

items.definition: The Greeks are a standard set of sensitivity measures describing how an option or portfolio's value responds to changes in an underlying factor.
items.core_idea: Each Greek answers a specific risk question (e.g., how much P&L results from a price move, a volatility change, time passing, or a rate change) and is always expressed as a relationship between an asset's value and some underlying driver, never as a standalone number.
key_points: Delta: P&L from a change in the price of the underlying asset.
Gamma: the change in delta itself as the underlying price changes.
Vega: P&L from a change in the underlying's volatility.
Theta: P&L from the passage of time, usually measured per day.
Rho: P&L from a change in the interest rate.
A Greek is always a comparison between two things — an asset and the underlying it's sensitive to — not a stand-alone figure like a price.
relationships: Delta and Gamma are first and second derivatives of price with respect to the underlying
trading_implications: Traders use the Greeks to answer practical risk questions, such as expected gain/loss if a price trend continues or if a low-probability event becomes more likely.

items.definition: Delta measures how much a portfolio's or option's value changes for a given change in the underlying's price; it is the first derivative of price with respect to the underlying.
items.core_idea: Delta is the most commonly used Greek, analogous to velocity in a car trip: just as velocity is the first derivative of distance with respect to time, delta is the first derivative of an option's value with respect to the underlying's price.
key_points: Delta can relate a portfolio's value to a broad benchmark (e.g., a stock portfolio to the S&P 500) or an option's value to its specific underlying.
The car-trip analogy: distance traveled relates to time similarly to how an option's value relates to the underlying price, with delta playing the role of velocity.
relationships: First derivative of price with respect to underlying
Gamma is the derivative of delta
trading_implications: Delta is the primary measure traders use to gauge directional exposure to the underlying.

items.definition: Gamma measures how much an option's delta changes as the underlying's price changes; it is the second derivative of price with respect to the underlying, analogous to acceleration.
items.core_idea: Although less directly informative than delta, gamma is closely watched by risk managers because it captures how a portfolio's risk profile itself shifts — becoming more or less exposed — when the underlying makes a large move.
key_points: Gamma is often considered more important than delta from a risk management standpoint.
It indicates whether a portfolio will become riskier or less risky as the market moves substantially.
Continuing the car-trip analogy, gamma is to delta what acceleration is to velocity.
relationships: Second derivative of price with respect to underlying
trading_implications: Risk managers scrutinize gamma to understand exposure during large or fast underlying price moves, not just small incremental ones.
common_misunderstandings: Assuming delta alone captures risk exposure; gamma reveals how that exposure itself changes under large market moves.
